I racked my brain for a while trying to come up with a neat link to another article to propose here, but with how tight knit the contents of this article is, it all came across as a little contrived. Then I stumbled upon Roget's tale Reversed Engineering in which these butterflies really shine, and felt that an inline link from this to that tale would be a good idea, especially when one considers how far out of the spotlight a lot of tales on the site remain. Suggesting the following edit:

Changing this:

When any adult instance of SCP-553 suffers significant damage, it produces a unique sonar signature which alerts all other nearby adults to the presence of danger. Adults will swarm the perceived source of danger and proceed to attack it by attempting to slice it with their wings. The wings of SCP-553 members have an average thickness of 5 mm where they attach to the body, and taper rapidly to any average thickness of 0.05 mm with sharp, beveled edges. In testing, individual lacerations as deep as 1 cm have been measured. However, deeper lacerations usually result in some portion of the wing structure breaking off in the inflicted wound. These fragments typically continue to fracture in the wound due to mechanical stresses. The circulatory fluid of SCP-553 reacts with most carbon-based tissues in a necrotizing fashion, resulting in significant post-traumatic infections.

To this:

When any adult instance of SCP-553 suffers significant damage, it produces a unique sonar signature which alerts all other nearby adults to the presence of danger. Adults will swarm the perceived source of danger and proceed to attack it by attempting to slice it with their wings. The wings of SCP-553 members have an average thickness of 5 mm where they attach to the body, and taper rapidly to any average thickness of 0.05 mm with sharp, beveled edges. In testing, individual lacerations as deep as 1 cm have been measured. However, deeper lacerations usually result in some portion of the wing structure breaking off in the inflicted wound. These fragments typically continue to fracture in the wound due to mechanical stresses. The circulatory fluid of SCP-553 reacts with most carbon-based tissues in a necrotizing fashion, resulting in significant post-traumatic infections.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Wow. Coming back to this after more than a year, it's clear how my tastes have changed. Although I like the idea of non-carbon-based life, there are so many just… wrong word choices here. For instance:

It appears to have no sensory organs, using a form of echolocation to view its surroundings

Echolocation is a sense, so therefore the butterflies have sensory organs. Hell, their entire bodies could be only large receiver for the echolocation. That kind of sensory perception is fairly common in sea creatures.

The life cycle is noticeable in that it appears more relatable to crystal growth rather than biological growth

*notable *"to be more closely related"

they will swarm around the intruder in an attempt to distract and/or injure the hostile

the hostile… what? I know you mean to use it as a noun, but it totally reads as an adjective. I suggest using "perceived threat" instead.

Finally, the harder something is, the more brittle it tends to be, especially stone. Given that the butterflies' wings are very, very thin by necessity, it should be incredibly easy to just snap them in two, no matter how sharp the edges are. In fact, just by lacerating something, the butterflies should be losing pieces off the edges whenever they strike bone or metal, maybe even just by lateral pressure on the wings if they try to pull them out at a different angle than they entered.

I had previously upvoted, but I'm afraid I;m going to have to remove that.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I was liking this one until the addendum, even with one being kept in an office. An organism that shouldn't exist by our understanding of life seems like the sort of thing the Foundation would attempt to contain, at least until they could explain how it exists.

That addendum kills it though, that changes it from "safe enough to be treated as a pet" to "RUN AWAY!" — and anything that causes a site to be destroyed should not be classified as safe (or kept as a pet). If it destroyed an entire site there's no way the Foundation would let one be kept in an office, nix that or the site destruction (or both).

Abstaining from voting until either that addendum is removed, or an incident report is added.

item.content:encoded:
Ok. So.

I am downvoting, at this point largely out of impatience. It's pretty clear at this point that it will be the incident report that would make or break this for me - an incident report that is absolutely needed to justify certain things about the SCP as written, and for which it has taken four days to put up a placeholder. This is one of the few places where the preference seems to be to "tell, not show" rather than "show, not tell," and if there's something about an SCP that needs a demonstration rather than a description to convey, I really kind of feel that it should be ready when the main writeup is posted, not hinted coyly at for half a week before being posted.

A really good incident report might sway me back in the other direction, but until it exists, I'm going to have to downvote.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I love the concept, but the article as it stands could use some work. Null vote for now, with probable upvote if the article improves.

The writing could use some cleanup. Two consecutive sentences in a row start with "It appears to…", and another sentence uses the phrase "in that" twice. Overall the description reads somewhat awkwardly, but I'm not sure how to fix that, and fixing the two glitches mentioned would help immensely.

You put a lot of stuff in the containment procedures that the description doesn't really explain. The humidity and temperature requirements are clearly to emulate 553's natural habitat, but why are the nutrients delivered in a water spray rather than just dumping a bag of sand? Also, I find it odd that a Safe-class SCP has requirements for the rooms and corridors around the containment unit. If that's really needed, I'd call this more of a Euclid-class. Also, why the low humidity and UV lamps? Those are not explained, and really should be.

Also also, agreed that the addendum is unnecessary and unhelpful.

This is one of those "would set the scientific world on it's ear!" things that happens every decade or so. Microbes from space/Mars (or so we thought), that live in volcanoes, life forms thought millions of years dead - all this has happened in my lifetime.

Points for "That's really different!" but in the end, it's 'just' a new lifeform.
